newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study looks at breast cancer gene education.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study looks at breast cancer gene education.

text.p: Education and counseling teach women the pros and cons of breast cancer genetic tests but apparently do little to influence their decisions about whether to get tested, researchers said Tuesday.

However, the women end up with a much more informed decision and a more realistic assessment of their own risks. The combination of education and counseling raised understanding better than education alone, they found.

"This does not mean that it has no effect but that people's decisions are more informed. They are more likely to go into the decision with an awareness of pitfalls and the outcomes of testing would be more favorable," said lead researcher Caryl Lerman, a psychologist at the cancer center of Georgetown University Medical Center in Washington.

Follow-up studies will examine women's subsequent cancer screening patterns and will see whether education and counseling better prepare women for the psychological stress if they do have a defective gene.

The study of 578 women with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer appears in Wednesday's edition of the Journal of the National Cancer Institute. It compared women who had education only, women who had education and counseling and a control group who had neither.
A specially trained nurse provided both components, neither of which tries to encourage or discourage testing.
The women had made decisions about testing before entering the study, and neither the education approach, nor the education and counseling combination, changed many minds.

The education session, roughly 45 minutes, provided objective facts about the BRCA1 breast cancer gene, the benefits and risks of testing, the possibility of insurance discrimination. The counseling session, about a half hour, added a more personal element about the specific woman's case.

"The counseling says, let's think about how you personally could be affected ... really addressing the issues on a more personal level to allow the person to deliberate more carefully on what effect is on them, on their family," Lerman told Reuters, noting that women tend to overestimate their risk for getting breast cancer.

BRCA1 carries a very high risk of breast and ovarian cancer but it is not the only cause of cancer. A woman who has the gene defect is very likely to get breast cancer at some time in her life but women without BRCA1 can still develop breast cancer. A second gene, BRCA2, has also been identified but tests are not available and less is known about the risk.

There is currently no way to prevent breast or ovarian cancer. Even surgically removing both breasts, which many doctors view as an extreme approach in most cases, may not totally guarantee a woman will not develop cancer. But early detection improves chances of surviving breast cancer.

Several biotech companies have made tests available. Lerman noted that most women's health advocacy groups and federal health officials have recommended that women who choose to get tested go through clinical trials at several sites in the country. Those trials include an educational component and the data does not get into a patient's medical records, which could affect insurance coverage.
